title: Duterte camp hit for using Truth Commission in defense
summary: The civil-society led Truth Commission has called out the defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte for using the initiative as part of its defense in the upcoming crimes against humanity…

blocks.text: November 29, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The civil-society led Truth Commission has called out the defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte for using the initiative as part of its defense in the upcoming crimes against humanity trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC).
In a statement, the commission disputed the Duterte camp’s claim that the body is a proof that “domestic mechanisms for accountability” exist in the Philippines.

“We exist because justice remains unfinished… We know of no Philippine government prosecution against Mr. Duterte for the crimes charged in The Hague. A truth commission would not have been needed if murders were being solved by the State one by one,” the civil society-led body said.

“Families came to us because official records were hard to obtain and their search for justice kept meeting obstacles. That citizens had to organize their own count of the dead is evidence of the gap, not of its repair,” it added.

Chaired by former ICC judge Raul Pangalangan, the commission was established to “document killings, listen to survivors and bereaved families, preserve evidence, examine patterns of violence and recommend paths to accountability, institutional reform, healing and non-recurrence.”

“Documenting a killing is not the same as prosecuting it… Civil society built this Commission to address a gap in accountability. To cite it as evidence that the gap has closed turns its purpose upside down,” it added.
In his pre-trial filing released on Thursday, Duterte’s lead defense counsel Peter Haynes cited the commission as an example of the supposed domestic mechanisms in the Philippines.
Haynes claimed Duterte did not commit any crimes against humanity and that the charges related to the killings should have been tried in the Philippines.

“The Philippines has a functioning criminal justice system, through which killings committed during the campaign against illegal drugs have been prosecuted, and continue to be prosecuted as ordinary murders,” the defense lawyer said in his filing.
Information about the Truth Commission were also included in the latest batch of evidence disclosed by the defense.
In its response to the defense filing, the Truth Commission maintained that its processes, while a pathway to justice, is not an alternative to it.

“We welcome genuine domestic investigations and prosecutions. Domestic and international accountability need not compete. But the voluntary work of civil society cannot stand in for the legal obligations of the State,” it said.
“Our existence does not absolve the State of its obligations, and it does not show that those responsible have been held to account,” it added.
The commission highlighted the small number of cases that reached the courts.

“Every conviction matters. But five cases set against thousands of documented deaths is not a functioning system of accountability. A full public accounting of convictions, acquittals, dismissals and pending cases is long overdue,” it said.
“The defense does not dispute that police committed unlawful killings during the drug war. That concession raises the question the brief never answers: where are the prosecutions?” added the body.

Duterte’s crimes against humanity trial will open tomorrow. He is facing charges over killings allegedly committed by the so-called Davao death squad, as well as those during this administration’s bloody war on drugs.
Meanwhile, a total of 7,990 personnel will be deployed by the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) tomorrow in anticipation of protests connected with Duterte’s first trial day.
The NCRPO will raise its status to full-alert level starting today, according to its spokesperson, Lt. Col. Hazel Asilo.
Tomorrow also marks the 163rd birth anniversary of Filipino hero Andres Bonifacio – a regular holiday across the country.
Asilo assured the public that police are “neutral” amid the politically charged events serving as backdrop for the rallies.

She reminded protesters not to go beyond designated freedom parks when conducting rallies to avoid the confrontations similar to what that occurred during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit, where over 200 people were arrested in separate protest actions.
